name: Germany's political history as the source of its philosophical absolutism
plain_explanation: Russell argues that strange-seeming features of German philosophy after Kant reflect the psychology of a proud but politically fragmented and repeatedly humiliated nation -- one that compensated in metaphysics and in eventual Prussian militarism for what it had lost in real-world power.
precise_definition: The thesis that post-Kantian German idealism's absolutist, anti-empirical direction -- and its later fusion with Prussian nationalism through Fichte and Hegel -- is causally connected to Germany's loss of the Holy Roman Empire's authority, its fragmentation after the Reformation and the Thirty Years' War, its humiliation by Napoleon at Jena, and its subsequent unification under Prussia by Bismarck.
why_it_mattered: It explains, for Russell, why German philosophy diverged so sharply from British empiricism and why figures like Fichte and Hegel became 'philosophic mouthpieces of Prussia.'
historical_origin: Drawn from Russell's reading of German history from Charles V through Bismarck.
associated_philosopher: Kant, Fichte, Hegel (as case studies), Bismarck (as political actor)
examples: Frederick the Great's failed attempt to make Berlin a cultural centre while neglecting economic and political reform
Bismarck's remark 'We will not go to Canossa' as a conscious invocation of the medieval imperial past
Kant's own liberal theology, which got him into trouble with the Prussian government, contrasted with Fichte's and Hegel's service to the Prussian state
influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up Russell's treatment of Hegel's glorification of the Prussian state in the next chapter.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: this concept is explicitly about the fusion of philosophy with German nationalism and Prussian state power.
